lead: An instruction is a coded command. The CPU fetches it as a pattern of bits and splits that pattern into fields. One field, the opcode, says what operation to perform. The rest, the operand or address field, says where the data is. The width and order of these fields is the instruction format, also called instruction encoding. Programmers never write these bits by hand; the assembler does it. Knowing the format explains why instruction lengths run from one byte on the 8085 up to six bytes on the 8086, why a PIC uses fixed 12- or 14-bit words, and why a jump needs more bytes than an increment.
prereq: You need: the stored-program idea and binary numbers from Unit 1, and the register names of the 8085 and 8086 from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Every instruction carries at least an opcode. Extra fields appear when the operation needs data. A register field is 3 bits wide on the 8085 and 8086, because 3 bits can name 8 registers. An immediate field holds the constant itself, inside the instruction. An address field holds a memory address, 16 bits on the 8085. The 8086 adds a ModRM byte, a single byte that names one register and says whether the other operand is a register or a memory location.

items: 8085: 1, 2 or 3 bytes. MOV A,B is 78H, one byte. MVI A,3FH is 3E 3F, two bytes. LDA 2000H is 3A 00 20, three bytes, address low byte first.
8051: 1 to 3 bytes. INC A is 04H; MOV A,#3FH is 74 3F; LJMP 2000H takes three bytes.
8086: 1 to 6 bytes. A ModRM byte, a displacement and an immediate may all follow the opcode.
PIC: fixed words of 12 bits (PIC12 family) or 14 bits (PIC16 family), so every instruction in these families is one word.

blocks.text: L = B_p + B_op + B_M + B_d + B_i
blocks.where: L is the instruction length in bytes; B_p is 0 to 3 prefix bytes (LOCK, REP, REPNE, segment override), each 1 byte; B_op is the opcode size (1 byte on the 8085, 8086 and 8051); B_M is a ModRM byte (0 or 1); B_d is a displacement (0, 1 or 2 bytes); B_i is an immediate (0, 1 or 2 bytes). On the 8086 the total, prefixes included, never exceeds 6 bytes.

sections.h3: Zero, one, two and three address formats

blocks.text: Formats are also named by how many operands an instruction may write down. Fewer operands mean shorter instructions but more instructions per job.

head: Format
Where operands live
Program for Z = A + B
rows: on a stack, popped two at a time
PUSH A; PUSH B; ADD; POP Z
LOAD A; ADD B; STORE Z
one operand doubles as the result

blocks.text: The 8086 and 8051 are two-address machines with the destination written first. On the 8085, MOV A,B names two registers with the destination first, but the arithmetic and logical instructions such as ADD B are one-address with A implicit (A ← A + B). Stack machines such as the Java virtual machine use the zero-address form, where the opcode alone is the whole instruction.
Instruction sets are grouped by what an instruction changes. Textbooks list five or six groups; the borders are not sharp, and one instruction may sit in two groups.

items: Data transfer: MOV, MVI, LDA, STA, IN, OUT, PUSH, POP. They move bits and leave the flags alone; PUSH and POP also change the stack pointer SP. See 3.3.
Arithmetic: ADD, ADC, SUB, INR, DCR, DAD on the 8085; MUL and DIV on the 8086. See 3.4.
Logical: ANA, ORA, XRA, CMP, RLC, RRC on the 8085; AND, OR, XOR, TEST on the 8086.
Branch and control transfer: JMP, JZ, JNC, CALL, RET, DJNZ. These can change the program counter. See 3.5.
Bit manipulation: SETB, CLR, CPL, JB, JNB on the 8051; the 8086 sets and tests single bits with logical instructions.
Machine control: HLT, NOP, EI, DI, SIM, RIM, WAIT on the 8085; the 8051 uses power-control bits instead of HLT.

blocks.text: A quick test while reading a listing: if only a register, memory cell or port changes, it is data transfer; if the program counter may change, it is a branch; if nothing in the program changes, it is machine control.

sections.h3: The four fields of an assembly statement

blocks.text: One line of assembly holds up to four columns.

blocks.code: LOOP:   MOV   A, B      ; copy B into A

items: Label: optional, starts in column one and ends with a colon. It marks this address so a branch can name it.
Mnemonic: the fixed name of the opcode, such as MOV or ADD. It comes from the manufacturer's table, not from the programmer.
Operand: zero to three items separated by commas; for two-address instructions the destination comes first.
Comment: everything after a semicolon. The assembler ignores it.

blocks.text: Translation of these four fields into machine code is the assembler's job, covered in 3.8.

figure.caption: The five working groups of one instruction set. Only the branch group, plus the bit-test jumps JB and JNB, can change the program counter; the rest change registers, memory, flags, or nothing at all.

examples.question: Encode these two instructions and state the length of each in bytes: (a) 8085 MVI A, 3FH; (b) 8086 MOV AX, BX.
steps: (a) The 8085 opcode for MVI A, move immediate to the accumulator, is 3EH. One byte.
The immediate value 3FH follows as the second byte, because the opcode has no room for 8 data bits.
Encoding: 3E 3F. Length = 1 opcode byte + 1 immediate byte = 2 bytes.
(b) MOV AX,BX uses the 8086 register-to-register form, opcode 89H, which means move a 16-bit register into a register or memory operand.
The next byte is ModRM. mod = 11 means both operands are registers. reg = 011 names BX, the source. r/m = 000 names AX, the destination. The byte is 11 011 000 = D8H.
No displacement and no immediate follow. Encoding: 89 D8. Length = 2 bytes.
examples.answer: Both instructions are 2 bytes long: 3E 3F for MVI A,3FH and 89 D8 for MOV AX,BX.
examples.check:
op = 0x3E
imm = 0x3F
enc_a = [op, imm]
mod, reg, rm = 0b11, 0b011, 0b000
modrm = (mod << 6) | (reg << 3) | rm
assert modrm == 0xD8
enc_b = [0x89, modrm]
print(len(enc_a))
print(len(enc_b))

traps: Later bytes are not opcodes. In 89 D8 the D8H is a ModRM byte; reading it as an opcode gives nonsense, and the 8086 length is not fixed.
Little-endian addresses: LDA 2000H assembles to 3A 00 20, not 3A 20 00. Writing the high byte first points at 0020H.
Mnemonic is not opcode. MOV and ADD are names the assembler translates; 78H and 89H are opcodes. Examiners often ask for the opcode of a given mnemonic.
One-address does not mean one operand. 8085 ADD B changes A and all the flags even though only B is written on the line.
PIC instruction words are 12 or 14 bits, not 8. A 14-bit instruction does not fit one 8-bit memory location.

quiz.q: Name the two parts of a general instruction format and say what each holds.
quiz.a: The opcode field says which operation to perform. The operand or address field says where the data is: a register number, an immediate constant, a memory address or a port address.

quiz.q: Why does the 8086 use a variable-length format while a PIC16 uses a fixed 14-bit word?
quiz.a: The 8086 must name 8 registers, 16-bit addresses and immediates of 1 or 2 bytes, so its fields differ in size and optional fields are added only when needed. A fixed word simplifies decoding but allows only small register and address fields.

quiz.q: Assemble 8085 LDA 2050H and give the length in bytes.
quiz.a: Opcode for LDA is 3AH. The address follows low byte first: 50H then 20H. Encoding 3A 50 20, length 3 bytes.

quiz.q: A 14-bit PIC instruction spends 7 bits on the register address and 1 bit on the destination. How many bits remain for the opcode?
In the encoding 89 D8, which register is the source and which is the destination? Show the bit split.
quiz.a: D8H = 1101 1000. mod = 11 (register to register), reg = 011 (BX), r/m = 000 (AX). Opcode 89H moves a register into r/m, so BX is the source and AX the destination: AX ← BX.

quiz.q: A student claims every 3-byte 8085 instruction contains a memory address. Is that right?
quiz.a: No. LDA 2000H has an address, but LXI H,2000H holds the data 2000H in the same two bytes, and JMP holds an address again. Byte count alone does not tell you what the last two bytes mean; the opcode decides.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real decoders are built to match these formats exactly: a fixed-length RISC machine such as ARM spends few transistors on decoding, while an x86 decoder must find instruction boundaries in a stream of variable-length bytes, which costs silicon and power. Newer curricula use RISC-V, whose six base formats (R, I, S, B, U, J) are a clean example of the same opcode-plus-fields idea. Search next for 'x86 instruction decoder', 'RISC-V instruction formats' and 'Thumb-2 16/32-bit encoding'.
